Recode numeric values with Stata-style rules

Source: R/recode.R
stata_recode.Rd

Recode individual values, sets, or closed numeric ranges using ordered rules.

  • stata_recode() (recode()): Keep unmatched values unless .default replaces them, and use named rules to assign value labels.

Usage

stata_recode(x, ..., .default = x)

recode(x, ..., .default = x)

Arguments

x

An integer or double vector, optionally a numeric haven::labelled() vector. Convert integer64 input explicitly before recoding.

...

Two-sided formulas values ~ code, applied in order. Each code is a single number or NA; name a rule to label its code. Expressions use the formula's environment, and stored formulas can be spliced with !!!.

.default

Replacement for unmatched elements: a single number, NA, or a vector as long as x. By default, keep the input values after SPSS user-missing codes have been converted to NA.

Value

An integer or double vector with the length and order of x. Named rules produce a haven::labelled() vector; otherwise the result is numeric without value labels. Names and the variable label are kept; previous value labels, SPSS missing-value metadata, and other input attributes are dropped. See Details for integer preservation.

Details

Matching rules

Rules apply to the original input, after SPSS missing-value conversion. The first match wins: 1 ~ 2, 2 ~ 1 swaps the codes. Unmatched values stay unchanged unless .default replaces them, including unmatched missing values.

The left side of a rule accepts:

  • a:b: A closed range, including decimals. Like Stata's a/b, 1:5 matches 4.5. Bounds must be single non-missing numbers in increasing order (equal bounds are allowed); lo:hi reads them from the formula's environment.

  • c(...): A combination of values and ranges, such as c(1, 3:5).

  • Other expressions: An evaluated set of values to match exactly. Missing selectors match all missing types, as described below.

Bare min and max on the left mean -Inf and Inf, not observed extrema: min:min does not select the smallest observed value. Calls such as min(x) evaluate normally. Bounds and value sets must use ordinary integer or double numbers; convert classed numbers such as integer64 explicitly.

Missing values and labels

Any missing selector matches NA, NaN and every tagged missing value. Thus NA ~ 0 and haven::tagged_na("a") ~ 0 both replace all missing types; individual tags cannot be selected separately. Unmatched tags survive when .default is omitted. SPSS user-missing codes and ranges become NA before matching, so their stored codes cannot be matched as ordinary numbers.

Old value labels are removed even if no values change. Named rules create new labels, including for unobserved codes. Labels and codes must correspond one-to-one, and missing codes cannot be labelled.

Output type

Integer input stays integer if all replacement codes and defaults are whole numbers within integer range: 1:5 ~ 1 does not force double output. Fractions, out-of-range values, infinities, NaN and tagged missing values require doubles; ordinary NA does not. Double input stays double, and the input is never modified.

Stata and other R functions

Use dplyr::mutate() to replace or create a variable (Stata's generate()), and dplyr::across() to recode several columns. Common translations are:

Stata ruleR rule or argument
(1/5 = 1)1:5 ~ 1
(1 3 7 = 0)c(1, 3, 7) ~ 0
(9 = .)9 ~ NA
(missing = 0)NA ~ 0
(else = .).default = NA
(1/5 = 1 "Low")Low = 1:5 ~ 1

These functions recode numeric values. For text, use dplyr::recode_values() or dplyr::replace_values() in dplyr 1.2.0 or later, or dplyr::case_match() in older versions. For factors, use forcats::fct_recode() or forcats::fct_collapse().

The alias recode() conflicts with dplyr::recode(). Use stata_recode() or an explicit namespace to avoid depending on which package was attached last.

See also

Other variable generation functions: as_dummy(), cut_quantile(), panel, row_egen, std()

Examples

# Keep unmatched values
x <- c(1, 4.5, 6, 9, 12, NA)
stata_recode(x, 1:5 ~ 1, 6:10 ~ 2)
#> [1]  1  1  2  2 12 NA

# Replace unmatched values with missing
stata_recode(x, 1:5 ~ 1, 6:10 ~ 2, .default = NA)
#> [1]  1  1  2  2 NA NA

# Unbounded intervals and missing values
stata_recode(x, min:5 ~ 0, 6:max ~ 1, NA ~ 9)
#> [1] 0 0 1 1 1 9

# Swap codes without cascading replacements
stata_recode(c(1, 2, 3), 1 ~ 2, 2 ~ 1)
#> [1] 2 1 3

# Assign new value labels
stata_recode(x, Low = 1:5 ~ 1, High = 6:max ~ 2)
#> <labelled<double>[6]>
#> [1]  1  1  2  2  2 NA
#> 
#> Labels:
#>  value label
#>      1   Low
#>      2  High

# Create a new variable
d <- data.frame(score = c(2, 7, 11))
dplyr::mutate(
  d,
  group = stata_recode(score, 1:5 ~ 1, 6:10 ~ 2, .default = NA)
)
#>   score group
#> 1     2     1
#> 2     7     2
#> 3    11    NA

# Apply rules to several variables and prefix the new names
items <- data.frame(item1 = c(1, 7, 9), item2 = c(3, 8, 12))
dplyr::mutate(
  items,
  dplyr::across(
    dplyr::everything(),
    function(v) stata_recode(v, 1:5 ~ 1, 6:10 ~ 2, 11:15 ~ 3),
    .names = "r_{.col}"
  )
)
#>   item1 item2 r_item1 r_item2
#> 1     1     3       1       1
#> 2     7     8       2       2
#> 3     9    12       2       3
